Se c . C
Ru l e ma k in g  Pr o c e d u r e
623
The problem stems from the way EP A chose to determine [per 
the Clean Air Act] which emissions “contribute [d] significantly” to 
downwind States’ difficulty meeting national ozone standards. Recall 
that EPA’s plan rested on an assumption that all 23 upwind States 
would adopt emissions-reduction tools up to a “uniform” level of 
“costs” to the point of diminishing returns. But as the apphcants ask: 
What happens—as in fact did happen—when many of the upwind 
States fall out of the planned FIP and it may now cover only a fraction 
of the States and emissions EPA anticipated? Does that affect * * * 
the point at which the remaining States might still “maxLniiz[e] cost- 
effectiv[e]” downwind ozone-level improvements? 87 Fed. Reg. 20055. 
As “the mix of states changes, ... and their particular technologies 
and industries drop out with them,” might the point at which 
emissions-control measures maximize cost-effective downwind air- 
quahty improvements also shift? Tr. of Oral Arg. 6.
Although commenters posed this concern to EPA during the 
notice and comment period, EPA offered no reasoned response. 
Indeed, at argument the government acknowledged that it could not 
represent with certainty whether the cost-effectiveness analysis it 
performed collectively for 23 States would yield the same results and 
command the same emissions-control measures if conducted for, say, 
just one State. Perhaps there is some explanation why the number 
and identity of participating States does not affect what measures 
maximize cost-effective downwind air-quafity improvements. But if 
there is an explanation, it does not appear in the final rule. As a 
result, the apphcants are likely to prevail on their argument * * * 
that the agency failed to supply “a satisfactory explanation for its 
action[,]” State Farm Mut. Automobile Ins. Co., 463 U.S. at 43, and 
that it instead ignored “an important aspect of the problem” before it, 
ibid.
Justice Barrett dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson. 
In her view, the majority misunderstood the EPA’s FIP:
Crucially, the final rule suggests that EPA calculated cost-
effectiveness thresholds based on the likely cost and impact of 
available emissions-reduction technology given national, industry-
wide data. Contrary to the Court’s speculations, these thresholds and 
the FIP’s resulting emissions limits appear not to depend on the 
number of covered States.
Justice Gorsuch responded to this point by noting that, “if the government had 
arguments along these lines, it did not make them” before the Supreme Court. 
In response to this. Justice Barrett retorted that the challenger states’ winning 
theory (that the FIP was premised on an assumption about the number of 
states covered) was “largely absent from the [states’] briefs” before the 
Supreme Court and “appear[ed] not to have crystallized until oral argument.
